title: Kernel contention introspective threshold sweep: field notes and microbench results
summary: Exploratory sweep to measure how mixed-kernel workloads create transient kernel contention and latency tails when INT8/AWQ variants are routed on the same GPU; includes microbench harness, headroom metric, and preliminary mitigation ideas.
content:
Purpose and motivation:

We keep seeing intermittent latency tail events in multi-tenant stacks where different model variants (AWQ vs GPTQ vs native FP32 paths) are co-located. Hypothesis: kernel-level contention and scheduling pressure (kernel launch overlap, memory lane conflicts, and device-side serialization points) create short stalls that disproportionately affect tail latencies even when average throughput looks fine. This doc records a focused sweep across contention thresholds, kernel mixes, and request shapes to surface systematic behaviors and candidate mitigations.

What is unique about this sweep:
- Introspection at kernel-launch granularity using lightweight counters + timestamps (not just host-side request/response).
- Synthetic mixed workloads that intentionally interleave short autoregressive calls (fast tokens) with long-context generation calls to provoke switching.
- A new headroom metric (TokenHeadroom) that combines available device compute cycles with queued kernel latency to quantify susceptibility to tail spikes.

Experiment harness (quick overview):
- Executor: local dev rig (A100-40GB, CUDA 12.3, driver 535.xx), runtime branch: kernel-contention-experiments-ashamehta.
- Models: distilled-350M (GPTQ int8 variant), llama-2-7b-awq (AWQ int8), baseline-3b-fp16. All served under same process via v2 routing shim.
- Client mix: 70% short-gen (prompt -> 32 tokens), 30% long-gen (prompt -> 1024 tokens). We vary short/long ratio 90/10 -> 50/50 in sub-sweeps.
- Concurrency: simulated steady-state QPS at 40, 80, 160. Batching disabled for short-gen to emphasize single-request kernel behavior; batching enabled for long-gen to keep throughput realistic.
- Instrumentation: nvtx ranges + nvprof style per-kernel start/end timestamps captured to file via lightweight agent. Host-side trace correlated with device counters (sm stalls, inst_issued) where available.

Key metrics captured:
- p50/p95/p99 token latency (host-observed)
- Kernel gap distribution (time between device kernel end and next kernel start on same stream)
- Device serialization events (approx from nvtx where kernels reported "stall_type=sm" or long memcpy spikes)
- TokenHeadroom = (estimated available SM cycles per second) / (measured cycles consumed per token) -> unitless; lower values indicate headroom exhaustion.
- Quality delta on a small eval set (BLEU-like for generation coherence) to ensure quantization variants still perform acceptably.

Representative run notes (5/15/2028):
- Baseline (single-variant FP16 only): p99 token latency = 142ms, TokenHeadroom = 3.8 at QPS 80. Kernel gap distribution concentrated near 0-2ms (steady streaming kernels).
- Mixed AWQ + FP16 (70/30 short/long, QPS 80): p99 jumped to 410ms. Device traces show bursts of queued memcpy and short kernel launches on alternative kernels that caused the FP16 long-gen stream to be preempted repeatedly. TokenHeadroom fell to 1.1 during bursts.
- GPTQ-int8 + AWQ-int8 mix (50/50, QPS 160): surprising micro-hop pattern: many tiny kernels (sub-ms) for AWQ pathway interleaving with slightly larger GPTQ kernels; p95 remained OK but p99 had a heavy tail (up to 1.2s) tied to occasional GC-like pauses on host pacing.

Interpretation and causal hypotheses:
1) Kernel diversity increases scheduling churn: many small kernels with heterogeneous occupancy profiles lead to more kernel launches and increased device-side scheduling overhead, particularly when memory copies are interspersed.
2) Memory lane contention: AWQ path uses extra activation packing/unpacking steps that issue asynchronous device->device copies; under load these cross-lane copies can block higher-occupancy kernels and manifest as serialization.
3) Host pacing and queuing: our single-process driver queues become hotspots when the client mix bursts; inadequate stream prioritization makes latency-sensitive short-gen suffer.

Interesting micro-observations (raw):
- On A100, some AWQ kernels run with low SM occupancy but high register pressure; they complete quickly but trigger a cascade of kernel dispatches that prevent larger FP16 kernels from launching immediately.
- When we forced AWQ kernels onto a different stream with CUDA stream priorities (high for FP16 long-gen), p99 improved by ~35% in the 80 QPS mixed run.
- Using cudaMemPrefetchAsync for activation buffers reduced memcpy spikes but introduced a new class of 3-6ms memcpy latencies when host pinned page faults occurred (rare but impactful).

Small ASCII table: consolidated p99 numbers (selected):

| mix | QPS | p99 token latency |
|-----|-----|-------------------|
| FP16 only | 80 | 142ms |
| AWQ+FP16 (70/30) | 80 | 410ms |
| GPTQ+AWQ (50/50) | 160 | 1200ms |
| GPTQ-int8 only | 160 | 260ms |
| AWQ-only | 160 | 340ms |

Mitigations tried (and notes):
- Stream prioritization: assign high priority stream to latency-sensitive short-gen. Result: consistent p99 improvement (20-40%) but does not eliminate long tails under extreme burst patterns.
- Kernel co-location rules: pin AWQ kernels to a dedicated CUDA context via separate process. Result: removes intra-GPU scheduling interference but reduces overall throughput by ~10% due to isolated resource partitions.
- Batching policy tweaks: enable micro-batching for short-gen (2-4 tokens) to reduce number of kernel launches. Result: average latency increases slightly but p99 improves in most mixes.
- Activation cache: keep a small on-GPU prefix cache to avoid repeated activation unpack copies for short-gen. Result: avoided several memcpy spikes; complexity added to runtime.

Open questions / things to validate:
- Are some of the observed memcpy spikes actually driver-level page migration artifacts? Need to re-run on pinned memory configs and evaluate with CUDA memquery and host kernel stacks.
- Quantify cost/benefit for separated process-per-variant approach: what commit size of throughput loss is acceptable for tail improvement?
- Can we design a lightweight kernel combiner that merges very small AWQ/GP kernels into fewer launches without changing model outputs? This seems hard but would massively reduce launch overhead.

Next experiments planned:
1) Repeat key sweeps on a V100 and H100 to compare cross-arch serialization modes. Record SM stall origins with Nsight Systems.
2) Add explicit prefetch/pin runs to isolate page-fault-induced memcpys.
3) Try streaming-multiplex shim: route latency-sensitive requests to a dedicated high-priority queue, low-latency throughput requests to background queue; measure queue overflow modes.
4) Implement a simple kernel-coalescing harness for AWQ tiny-kernel chains and measure impact on p99.

Actionable quick wins (for runtime team):
- Introduce stream priority knobs in runtime routing config (expose via per-route config in console).
- Add an optional "activation cache" toggle for short prompts to avoid repeated pack/unpack memcpy across requests.
- Provide operational guidance: when onboarding AWQ models, recommend dedicated worker pools or lower-density co-location with high-occupancy FP kernels.

Notes to self / todo:
- Push the instrumentation branch and attach sample nvtx traces to JIRA-8132.
- Run long-duration soak (12h) with production-like traffic to validate no regression on throughput after isolations.
- Draft a short troubleshooting playbook for SREs explaining kernel-contention fingerprints and quick heuristics to triage.

Appendix: short checklist for reproducing locally
- Checkout branch: kernel-contention-experiments-ashamehta
- CUDA driver: 535.86, CUDA toolkit 12.3
- Model artifacts: /mnt/models/{distilled-350m-gptq, llama2-7b-awq, baseline-3b-fp16}
- Run harness: scripts/run_mixed_sweep.sh --qps 80 --short_ratio 0.7 --concurrency 64 --trace nvtx

End of notes.

If this resonates with others who have seen odd p99s, drop quick replication notes in the thread or ping me.
